report:
**Conclusion: your “no” is too definite.** For children **older than 12 months** with an acute cough from a cold/upper-respiratory infection, honey *may* provide modest short-term symptom relief—especially less frequent/severe night cough and better sleep—versus no treatment, placebo, or some cough medicines. NICE summarizes reductions of roughly 0.5–2 points on a parent-reported 7-point cough scale after one day. [https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng120/chapter/summary-of-the-evidence](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng120/chapter/summary-of-the-evidence)

But the evidence is limited: trials are small, primarily measure parent-reported symptoms, often assess only one night, and evidence certainty ranges from low to moderate. Cochrane’s review finds honey probably reduces cough frequency compared with no treatment/placebo, but says there is **no strong evidence** either for or against its use overall. It is not proven to cure the infection, prevent complications, or reliably shorten illness. [https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094_honey-acute-cough-children](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094_honey-acute-cough-children)

A 2023 systematic review likewise concluded that low-quality evidence suggests honey may beat cough medicines or placebo/no treatment for symptoms and sleep, while calling for better blinded, placebo-controlled trials. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37355498/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37355498/)

**Important exception:** never give honey to a child **under 12 months**, because it can cause infant botulism. [https://www.cdc.gov/infant-toddler-nutrition/foods-and-drinks/foods-and-drinks-to-avoid-or-limit.html](https://www.cdc.gov/infant-toddler-nutrition/foods-and-drinks/foods-and-drinks-to-avoid-or-limit.html)

Seek medical care for breathing difficulty, bluish lips, dehydration, unusual sleepiness, or a concerning/persistent cough.
